textual_basis: "At 847e-848b, the Athenian turns to food and distribution of what comes from the land and says an arrangement near the correctness of Cretan law seems fitting. Everyone must divide all that comes from the land into twelve parts according to how it is to be consumed. Each twelfth part, such as wheat and barley and all other seasonal produce following them, together with all animals saleable in each part, is divided three ways according to ratio: one part for free persons, one for their household slaves, and the third for craftsmen and all foreigners, including resident aliens needing necessary food and those arriving for some public or private need. This third share alone is necessarily saleable, while nothing from the two other shares must be sold."
limits: "This records the twelvefold and threefold distribution rule. It does not include village settlement and market oversight."
review_status: accepted

textual_basis: "At 860d-860e, the Athenian asks how their own account stands with consistency and restates that all bad people are altogether bad unwillingly. From this it follows that the unjust person is bad, and the bad person is such unwillingly; what is involuntary cannot reasonably be done voluntarily. Thus the wrongdoer would appear to do wrong unwillingly to someone who posits injustice as involuntary, and the Athenian says he agrees that all do wrong unwillingly, despite possible claims that some are unwillingly unjust but willingly do wrong from love of victory or honor. He then frames the question of Magnesian legislation: whether to legislate at all, and whether to define voluntary and involuntary injustices with larger penalties for voluntary cases and smaller ones for involuntary cases, or equal penalties because no injustices are voluntary at all."

Before assigning penalties, they must show that there are two relevant kinds and define their difference; otherwise no one can judge whether a penalty has been fittingly set. He refuses to suppress the involuntary-injustice thesis, but says the two kinds must differ by something other than voluntary and involuntary in the usual way."
textual_basis: "At 861a-861d, Clinias asks how to use the present claims. The Athenian recalls that they had just said there is much disturbance and discord about just things, and asks whether, without finding a way through and defining how these differ, they can legislate as though all lawgivers everywhere correctly posit two kinds of injustices, voluntary and involuntary. He rejects merely uttering a godlike thesis without explanation and says it is necessary before legislation to make clear that the two kinds exist and that their difference is otherwise, so that when a penalty is attached to either kind everyone can follow and judge the fittingness of the enactment. Clinias says they must either stop saying all injustices are involuntary or first define why that claim is correct. The Athenian refuses not to say what he thinks true, since that would not be lawful or holy, and says they must try to show the two kinds by some other difference."
limits: "This records the methodological demand for definition before penalty law. It does not include the harm-versus-injustice distinction introduced next."

observation: "The Athenian distinguishes harms from injustices: voluntary and involuntary elements abound in civic interactions, but not every harm is an injustice. Unwilled harm is not to be legislated as involuntary injustice, while wrongly produced benefit can still be unjust; the legislator must look both to injustice and to harm, restoring damaged things where possible and using compensation to move doers and sufferers from conflict toward friendship."
textual_basis: "At 861e-862c, the Athenian says many harms arise among citizens in associations and dealings, and voluntary and involuntary elements are abundant in them. He warns against treating all harms as injustices and then dividing injustices into voluntary and involuntary, since involuntary harms are not fewer than voluntary harms in number or magnitude. He says he will not call it injustice when someone harms another unwillingly and not wanting to do so, and will not legislate that as an involuntary injustice, whether the harm is larger or smaller. Conversely, if his account prevails, a person can do injustice by being the cause of a benefit that is not rightly produced. Giving or taking away something should not simply be called just or unjust; the legislator must look to whether someone benefits or harms another by using character and a just manner, and must look to both injustice and harm. The harmed thing should be made sound by laws as far as possible, saving what is lost, setting upright what is fallen, making sound what is killed or wounded, and after compensation for each harm, trying always to establish doers and sufferers from difference into friendship."
limits: "This records the distinction between harm and injustice and the restorative aim of law. It does not include the next claim about curing unjust harms as diseases in the soul."
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: "At 863b-863e, the Athenian says they already hear and say that in the soul there is spirit, whether passion or part, naturally implanted as a contentious and hard-fighting possession that overturns many things by irrational force. He distinguishes pleasure from spirit and says pleasure rules from an opposite power by persuasion with deception, doing whatever its wish wants. He then names ignorance as a third cause of errors. A better lawgiver divides it in two: simple ignorance is the cause of light errors, while double ignorance occurs when someone is held not only by ignorance but by the opinion of wisdom, as if he knew completely what he does not know at all. With strength and force this causes great and unmusical errors; with weakness it causes errors of children and elders, for which the laws should be gentlest and most full of pardon."
limits: "This records the tripartite source account and the twofold ignorance distinction. It does not include the following formal definition of injustice."

textual_basis: "At 864a-864c, the Athenian says that since three kinds of errors have been disclosed, they should be recalled more firmly. One kind is pain, which they call spirit and fear; a second is pleasure and desires; a third is the pursuit of hopes and true opinion concerning the best. When this third itself is split, the three become five kinds, and laws differing from one another must be set for the five kinds in two classes. The classes are actions done through violent and manifest acts, and acts done secretly with darkness and deception; sometimes a deed is done through both, and in such cases laws would be harshest if they had their fitting share."

  At 865d-866a, the speaker says that someone who unwillingly kills a free person must undergo the same purifications as the killer of a slave, and he says not to dishonor an old story. The story presents the violently killed free person as angry, fearful, and disturbing the killer when the killer remains in familiar places. For this reason the killer must withdraw for all seasons of the year, empty all familiar places of the homeland, and, if the dead person was a foreigner, be barred from that foreigner's country for the same period.
limits: >-
  This record reports the stated purification, story, and absence requirement. It does not treat the story as an independent doctrine or cover the doubled penalties for disobedience.

observation: "A parent-killer acting from anger receives different treatment depending on release by the dying parent. Release lets the killer follow the involuntary-homicide purification pattern and become clean; without release, the act is placed under assault, impiety, and sacrilege, and death is prescribed because the law will not permit even lethal self-defense against parents."
textual_basis: "At 869a-869c, the speaker describes someone uncontrolled by anger toward parents. If the dying parent willingly releases the killer before death, the killer is purified like those who committed involuntary homicide and becomes clean. If there is no release, the killer is liable to the severest assault suits, impiety, and sacrilege, and the span argues that no law grants permission to kill father or mother even when one is about to die at parental hands, ending with death as the penalty for killing father or mother in anger."
limits: "This record covers the anger case against parents. It does not cover premeditated parental murder or the later self-defense rules for non-parental cases."
review_status: accepted
```

observation: "The amount of penalty discretion delegated to courts depends on the quality of the courts. Base, secretive, noisy courts should receive only the smallest discretion while the lawgiver states most penalties directly; well-established courts with educated and tested judges may judge many matters about what offenders should suffer or pay. For the present law code, the Athenian proposes giving judges the greatest and largest matters while still supplying outlines, types, and examples so judgment does not step outside justice."
textual_basis: "At 876b-876e, the Athenian contrasts defective courts that conceal opinions or judge noisily like theaters with courts correctly established as far as possible, whose future judges have been well educated and carefully tested. In the first kind of city, he says only the smallest penalty decisions should be entrusted to courts while the lawgiver states most matters explicitly. In the better case, it is proper to entrust many decisions about what offenders should suffer or pay. He then says their present judges can receive the greatest and most numerous matters, provided the lawgiver gives outlines, types, and examples of penalties so they never go outside justice."
limits: "This records the court-discretion rule and its safeguards. It does not give the later specific wound penalties that follow after the return to the laws."
review_status: accepted

The rewards and penalties include front seats at contests, perpetual exile, praise, blame, freedom, one hundred lashes administered by the marketplace, city, or country officials depending on location, and a curse for the local person who does not defend."

It assigns country-wardens to punish a violator of the exclusion and death for coming down into the city. The same span says free persons who share food, drink, association, or even voluntary touch with such a person must not enter shrine, marketplace, or city before purification, because they have shared in a polluting fortune. It also makes a non-prosecuting official answerable in audits if he notices the offender polluting sacred things and the city."
limits: "This records the post-conviction exile, contact-pollution, and official-audit rules. It does not include the separate slave-on-free assault law introduced at the end of the span."

Those present bind the slave with the person struck and deliver him to the injured party, who binds him in fetters, whips him as many times as desired without harming the master, and gives him back to the owner. The owner who receives him bound must not release him until the slave persuades the struck person that he is worthy to live unbound; the text then extends the same rules across female-female and female-male cases."
limits: "This records the slave-on-free assault procedure and its gender extension. It does not include the prior parent-assault pollution rule that overlaps the opening of 882a."

```yaml

greek_terms: [γενέσεως, φθορᾶς, αἴτιον, ψυχήν, πρώτοις, σωμάτων, μεταβολῆς, νοῦς, τέχνη, νόμος, φύσιν]
english_gloss: "generation, destruction, cause, soul, among first, bodies, change, intellect, art, law, nature"
feature_family: soul_priority_argument
feature_id: feature_candidate_4135
feature_label: soul_priority_reorders_nature_art_law_and_body
observation: "The counterargument says the impious accounts invert priority: what is first cause of generation and destruction is made later, and what is later is made prior. Soul must be understood as among the first things, older than bodies, and ruling their changes; therefore opinion, care, intellect, art, and law are prior to bodily qualities, and if soul is first, nature is more properly said of soul than of fire or air."
textual_basis: "At 891e-892c, the Athenian says the speeches forming impious souls have made the first cause of generation and destruction later, and the later thing prior, causing error about the being of gods. He explains that almost everyone is ignorant of soul, especially its generation and power: soul is among the first things, comes before all bodies, and especially rules all their change and reordering. From this he says things kindred to soul, including opinion, care, intellect, art, and law, would be prior to hard, soft, heavy, and light. He adds that if soul is shown to be prior, then nature is most correctly said of soul rather than fire or air."
limits: "This records the priority argument up to the announced need to prove soul older than body. It does not include the later motion proof itself."
review_status: accepted
```

Applying the analogy, he says the coming argument may be stronger and nearly impassable for their strength, so he should question himself first, answer himself again, and carry the whole argument through until it completes the account of soul and shows soul before body."

textual_basis: "At 896e-897b, the argument asks whether what is moved in every way must govern heaven, posits more than one soul, and lists the soul-motions that take up secondary bodily motions into growth, wasting, separation, combination, and sensible qualities. The same span distinguishes soul with intellect from soul joined with folly."
limits: "This records the causal setup for soul's governance. It does not decide yet which kind of soul governs the visible heavenly circuit."
review_status: accepted
```

He then says a post-prelude speech should rightly interpret the laws by ordering impious people to change to pious ways. For those not persuaded, he states the law: if someone is impious in speech or deed, a bystander must report to officials; the first officials who hear must bring the case to the appointed court according to the laws; an official who hears and fails to act is liable to prosecution for impiety."

When a craftsman sells such a person to a private buyer, the buyer has six months to return, except for the sacred disease where the period is one year; selected doctors judge the case, and the losing seller pays double the price. On this basis he says he will not willingly allow someone, by flatteries during illness or unstable old age, to persuade them to dispose contrary to the best, but will legislate looking to what is best for the whole city and family."

If a son remains not made upon an allotment and is legally expected to be sent to a colony, the father may give him as much as he wishes from the remaining property except the ancestral allotment and its equipment; if there are several, he divides surplus as he wishes. He should not assign money to a son who already has a household, nor to a daughter already betrothed, but should assign to an unbetrothed daughter. If after the will a local allotment appears for a son or daughter, it is left to the heir; if there are no males but daughters, he writes as heir the husband of whichever daughter he wishes, leaving him as his son."

textual_basis: "At 928b-928d, an official may penalize a guardian who acts contrary to the law, while a guardian may bring the official into the selected court for a double assessment. After reaching youth, an orphan may bring a guardianship suit within five years after the guardianship ends. If an official harms the orphan through neglect, the court assesses payment to the child; if through injustice, he is removed from the office of law-guardian and replaced by the city."

In this city, a disowned child must emigrate because the fixed number of households admits no additional household, so the law requires severance by the whole kin-group rather than by one father alone."
textual_basis: "At 928d-929a, the Athenian says disputes between fathers and children can exceed what is needed, with fathers wanting authority to publicly renounce a son and sons wanting authority to prosecute fathers for madness when disease or old age has made them behave shamefully. He says such things arise in very bad characters, and that in another regime a disowned child would not necessarily be without a city. In the present regime the fatherless person must settle in another land because no one may be added to the five thousand and forty households; therefore the person about to suffer this must be renounced in legal process by the whole kin-group, not by one father."
limits: "This records the rationale for requiring kin-group process in disowning. It does not include all procedural voting requirements, which are stated in the following span."
review_status: accepted

observation: "A father who wants to sever a son from his kinship may not do it immediately or lightly. He must gather his own relatives up to cousins and the son's maternal relatives, make his accusation before them, allow the son equal speeches in reply, and obtain more than half of the adult relatives' votes, excluding the father, mother, and accused son from the vote."
textual_basis: "At 929a-929c, the law says that if anger, whether justified or not, leads a father to desire to remove the son he begot and raised from his kinship, it must not be permitted easily or at once. First he must collect his relatives up to cousins and likewise the son's relatives on the mother's side. He accuses before them, teaching that the son deserves expulsion from the kin-group, and gives the son equal speeches to show he deserves none of this. If the father persuades them and gains more than half the votes of all adult relatives, with father, mother, and accused son excluded, then and only then may he disown the son."
limits: "This records the hearing and voting threshold for disowning. It does not include the later adoption and colony fallback for a disowned son."
review_status: accepted
```

  children receives advisory, not compulsory, guidance to raise them without

The passage adds that the nature of such things is not easy to know or to persuade others about, and it names wax images placed at doors, crossroads, and parental tombs as cases where simple dismissal is not persuasive without a clear doctrine."

The stated aim is future correction, not undoing the past event, and the judge is described as helping the lawgiver when a law leaves penalty assessment to the court."
textual_basis: "At 933e-934c, the speaker says that someone who harms another by theft or force pays more for greater harm and less for lesser harm, in an amount matching the harm until the damaged thing is healed. Each wrongdoing also receives a corrective penalty: the passage distinguishes lighter and heavier causes, states that punishment is not paid because the deed can become undone, and gives future aims such as hating injustice or easing the condition. It then says the judge must assist the lawgiver when the law entrusts the assessment of what the defendant must suffer or pay."
limits: "This records the general penalty theory attached to theft and violence. It does not supply the later itemized penalties for every particular theft or violent act."

observation: "The abusive-speech law gives a universal prohibition against reviling and redirects verbal dispute into teaching and learning for the disputants and those present. Its rationale is that curses and shameful names turn light words into serious hatred and enmity, feed anger, and undo the gentling produced by education."
textual_basis: "At 934e-935a, the law says no one is to revile anyone. It says disputants in arguments should teach and learn from one another and from those present while altogether abstaining from reviling. The explanation says that mutual curses and shameful names make serious hatreds and enmities arise from words, feed anger with bad nourishment, and make savage again the part of the soul that had once been gentled by education."
limits: "This records the speech rule and its stated psychological rationale within the cited span. It does not include whatever further transition begins after the final incomplete phrase at the end of 935a."
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: "At 936b-936c, the Athenian says the pitiable person is not simply someone hungry or similarly afflicted, but a moderate person, or someone with virtue or part of it, who also has some misfortune. He says it would be astonishing if such a person were entirely neglected into the last poverty in a moderately governed city. Therefore the lawgiver may safely set a law: no beggar is to come into being in the city. If someone attempts this by gathering a life with ineffective prayers, market officials remove him from the market, city officials from the town, and rural officials send him from the rest of the country to the border so the land is wholly clean of such a creature."

textual_basis: "At 936c-936e, the Athenian says if a male or female slave damages another person's property, without the injured party being partly responsible through ignorance or some unwise use, the master of the damaging slave must either cure the damage fully or hand over the slave. If the master accuses the injured party of a joint trick with the slave to deprive him of the slave, he is to litigate bad craft against the claimant; if he wins he receives double the value of the slave as assessed by the court, and if he loses he repairs the damage and hands over the slave. The same payment rule applies when a pack animal, horse, dog, or other livestock injures a neighbor's property."
limits: "This records liability for slaves and animals causing damage. It does not include later witness rules."

One called as a witness who does not meet the caller is liable for the damage. A witness raised by a judge does not vote in that case. A free woman may testify and advocate if over forty, and may bring a suit if without a husband; if her husband is alive she may testify only. A female slave, male slave, or child may testify and advocate only for homicide, if a reliable guarantor is provided that the person will remain until trial if accused of false testimony."

textual_basis: "At 937b-937d, each litigant may object to all or part of testimony before judgment if he claims someone testified falsely; officials keep the sealed objections from both parties for the judgment on false testimony. If someone is twice convicted of false testimony, no law compels him to testify; if three times, he is no longer permitted to testify, and if he dares to testify after three convictions anyone may denounce him to the official, who hands him to a court, with death as the penalty if convicted. If testimonies convicted as false seemed to have produced victory for the successful party, and more than half such testimonies are condemned, the case lost on these testimonies becomes subject to retrial and dispute over whether it was decided by them; however that issue is decided, it settles the earlier suits."
limits: "This records false-witness objection, disqualification, capital sanction, and retrial mechanism. It does not include the following critique of corrupt legal advocacy."

If justice is fine, co-advocacy would also be fine. But a certain badness slanders these things by attaching the fine name of craft to itself; it claims to be a device of lawsuits, able both to litigate and advocate for another and to win whether the matters in the case have been justly or unjustly done, and it gives the craft and its speeches as a gift in exchange for money."

For those who disobey, the law says anyone may indict a person who seems to try to turn the power of just things in judges' souls toward the opposite, litigate out of season over such matters, or co-advocate badly; he is tried in the court of selected judges. If convicted, the court assesses whether he acts from love of money or love of victory. For love of victory, the court sets how long he may not bring suit or advocate; for love of money, a foreigner must leave and never return or die, while a citizen dies for honoring gain from every direction; if twice judged to act this way from love of victory, he dies."

It says the law does not punish either because of the lesser or greater size of the theft, but because one may still be curable and the other incurable. It then assigns court assessment to a foreigner or slave caught stealing public property, but death to a citizen, raised as he is expected to have been raised, who is caught plundering or violently seizing the fatherland, whether caught in the act or not."

observation: "A person enrolled or assigned to military service must serve, and absence through cowardice without release by generals is tried as nonservice before the military authorities when they return from camp. The judges are those who actually served, divided by military class, and conviction bars the offender from future contests for overall military excellence, from accusing another of nonservice, and from acting as prosecutor in such cases, while leaving further penalty to the court."
textual_basis: "At 943a-943b, the law says that the enrolled person or the person assigned to some part must serve. If someone leaves out through cowardice without the generals releasing him, charges of nonservice go to the military officials when they return from camp. Each class of those who served judges separately: hoplites judge hoplites, horsemen judge horsemen, and the others likewise judge their own military associates. If someone is convicted, he may never become a contestant for overall excellence, never write up another for nonservice, and never be prosecutor about these matters; the court also assesses what he must suffer or pay."
limits: "This records the nonservice procedure and disabilities. It does not cover the separate award process that follows after these trials."
review_status: accepted

Plaintiffs and defendants write accusations and denials without oath, because frequent lawsuits would otherwise create widespread perjury among people who continue to share civic and private life; by contrast, judges, public office selectors, sacred voters, and contest officials may still use oaths where human opinion sees no profit in perjury."
textual_basis: "At 948d-949a, the passage says intelligent lawgivers should remove oaths from both litigants at the conclusion of lawsuits: the accuser writes charges without adding an oath, and the defendant submits a written denial unsworn. It gives the reason that in a city with many lawsuits nearly half the people would knowingly be perjured while still mixing in common meals and private associations. The next law keeps oaths for judges, those establishing public offices, sacred voting, and contest officials in music, gymnastic, and equestrian matters, but says cases where denial and swearing appear to bring large gain are to be judged without judicial oaths between litigants."

observation: "The approved young observers become special objects of civic surveillance: the city honors those who turn out well and dishonors failures more sharply than others. A returning traveler who has observed foreign customs must report any findings about laws, education, or nurture to the whole council; if he returns improved he is praised and honored, but if corrupted he is barred from social influence and can be executed if he meddles with education and laws after disobeying officials."
textual_basis: "At 952b-952d, the Athenian says the whole city must watch approved young men, honor those who succeed, and dishonor those who turn out worse than the many. One who has observed customs among other peoples must immediately go to the council and share any report about lawmaking, education, or nurture, or anything he himself has noticed. If he appears neither worse nor better he is praised for zeal, if much better he receives greater praise while alive and fitting honors after death, and if corrupted he must not associate with young or old while pretending wisdom. If he obeys officials he lives privately; if not, and if convicted in court of meddling with education and laws, he dies."
limits: "This records the screening of returning civic observers. It does not include the subsequent classification of incoming foreigners."
review_status: accepted

He then says all foreign men and women from another country are to be received, and the city's own sent out, according to these laws, honoring Zeus of strangers, not making exclusions by foods and sacrifices as the Nile herds do now, nor by savage proclamations."
limits: "This records the xenia closure to the visitor laws. It does not include the following guarantee and search statutes."
review_status: accepted
```

If someone does not allow a searcher to search, the excluded person may sue after valuing the item sought, and a convicted person pays double the assessed damage. If the householder is away, residents provide unsealed items for search; sealed items are sealed over and a guardian appointed for five days by the searcher. If the householder is away longer, the searcher takes the city officials, opens sealed things, and then reseals them in the same way with the household members and city officials."

textual_basis: "At 954c-954e, the Athenian gives a time limit for disputable things after which possession may no longer be challenged. He says there is no such dispute about lands and dwellings here. For other things, if someone is seen using what he possesses in city, market, and temples, and no one lays claim while another says he is seeking it, if a year passes the possession may not be challenged. If it is not used in city or market but openly in the fields and no claimant appears within five years, after five years it may no longer be challenged. If someone uses it in houses in town, the limit is three years; if possessed hidden in the fields, ten years; if in another country, there is no time limit on laying claim whenever it is discovered."
limits: "This records property-claim limitation periods. It does not include forceful obstruction of lawsuits or contests."

If someone forcefully prevents a rival in gymnastics, music, or another contest from appearing, anyone may report it to the contest judges, who are to release the would-be competitor into the contest. If they cannot, and the blocker wins, the prizes are to be given to the blocked competitor and he is to be inscribed as victor in any temples he wishes; the blocker may make no dedication or inscription for that contest and is liable for damage whether he loses or wins."
limits: "This records forceful obstruction of trials and contests. It does not include receiving stolen goods or private war and peace."

observation: "After the burial rules, the speaker marks the legislation as nearly complete but says completion requires finding preservation for what has been generated. textual_basis: "At 960b-960e, the passage says other burial and no-burial cases for parricides, temple robbers, and similar people have already been set down, so the legislation almost has an end. It then defines the end of a whole not as doing, acquiring, or settling something, but as finding complete preservation for what has been generated; before that, the whole is incomplete. The discussion turns to the names of the Fates and especially the irreversible power associated with Atropos, and asks how such power must come to the laws according to nature. Clinias urges not leaving until this is secured for the stated laws."
limits: "This records the transition from completed statutes to the problem of preserving the laws. It does not identify the preserving institution, which begins in the next marker."

  The political art is pressed with the same demand made of other arts: it must say what single target it looks to. The example chosen is virtue, which had been divided into four kinds but is also named as one thing, so the interlocutors must explain both the distinct names and the common name.
textual_basis: >-
  At 963b-963e the Athenian turns from pilot, medical, and generalship examples to the political case and asks what the one object is that political intellect looks toward. When Clinias and Megillus cannot articulate it, he says they must try to see it, beginning from the four kinds of virtue. Each of the four must be called one, yet all together are called by one name, virtue; the difference that gives courage and prudence different names is easier than saying how both, and the others, share the common name virtue.
limits: >-
  This supplements the surrounding records on intellect leading virtue and the courage-prudence distinction. It does not supply the final answer to the unity question.

observation: >-
  The closing discussion reverses the common suspicion that astronomy and its allied arts make practitioners atheistic. The harmful form of the study is traced to treating heavenly motions as necessities without purposive thought and to treating the visible heavens as soulless bodies that assign causes to the cosmos.
textual_basis: >-
  At 967a-967d the Athenian reports that many suppose astronomy and the necessary arts connected with it make people atheistic because such students see events as produced by necessities rather than by deliberative purposes concerning goods. He then says the present position is the opposite: earlier investigators wondered how soulless bodies could use such exact calculations, some dared to say intellect orders the heavens, but the same people erred by making soul younger than bodies, with the result that the visible heavenly things appeared full of stone, earth, and other soulless bodies distributing the causes of the cosmos. He identifies that earlier account as producing many atheisms, difficulties, and poetic abuse of philosophers.
limits: >-
  This records the diagnostic reversal about astronomy and atheism. It does not yet state the positive educational requirements for rulers.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: >-
  The Athenian denies that the decisive details of the nocturnal council can yet be legislated in writing. The institution must be constructed through teaching and much association, beginning with a list of suitable people by age, learning capacity, character, and habit; written schedules of what and when to learn are called useless before knowledge of the timely moment arises in the learner's soul.
textual_basis: >-
  At 968c-968e the Athenian says it is no longer possible to legislate laws about such matters before the council has been ordered; only then will the members legislate authoritatively about what they must govern. For now, what constructs such things would come through teaching with much association if it comes correctly. He says first a list must be drawn of those suited to the guard by age, powers for learning, character, and habits. He adds that what must be learned is hard to discover and hard to learn from another, and that writing down the times and occasions for each item is vain, since the learners themselves would not know that it is being learned at the right moment until knowledge has come to be inside each soul.
limits: >-
  This records the stated non-written and association-based formation process. It does not infer a general doctrine about all writing.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: >-
  At 927e the Athenian says that if they lacked moderately stated laws about these same matters, there would be reason to set down special guardianship laws as greatly different and to diversify orphan life with private practices beside that of non-orphans. But as things stand, orphanhood among them is not very different from the father-regulated condition in all such matters, while in honors, dishonors, and forms of care it is not apt to be made equal.
limits: >-
  This records the rationale for not making a wholly separate orphan way of life. It does not include the following guardian standard or penalty procedure.
review_status: accepted
```
